title: Global Water Casebook — validated hydrology lessons
purpose: Reference set for comparing water loss, degraded connectivity, sedimentation, diversion, groundwater pressure, drought, natural variability and restoration patterns against the Olszówka/Gardeja testbed. Cases are not automatic diagnoses for Olszówka.

validation_policy.validated_case: At least one official/public source supports the stated mechanism.
validation_policy.candidate_case: May be queued for later review but must not be presented as confirmed.
validation_policy.intervention_notice: Engineering actions require local hydrological, ecological, legal and safety assessment before any field work.

cases.name: Aral Sea
cases.observed_pattern: Major shrinkage after diversion of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya for irrigation.
cases.management_lesson: Track the complete inflow network and water abstractions; restoration can depend on targeted flow-management and hydraulic interventions rather than lake-only actions.

cases.name: Lake Chad
cases.observed_pattern: Large long-term area and depth reduction accompanied by silting and sedimentation.
cases.management_lesson: Separate climatic inflow decline from local channel silting and sediment transport; both can reduce effective storage and connectivity.

cases.name: Hamoun wetlands
cases.observed_pattern: Wetland collapse followed a combination of reduced Helmand River inflow and drought.
cases.management_lesson: Do not classify a drying wetland as drought-only until upstream diversions, dams and river-flow losses are checked.

cases.name: Lake Poopó
cases.observed_pattern: A shallow lake effectively dried after recurrent drought and diversion of water sources.
cases.management_lesson: Shallow lakes can cross critical thresholds quickly; inflow time series and shoreline recession should be monitored together.

cases.name: Lake Urmia
cases.observed_pattern: Severe shrinkage associated with blocked/reduced inflows and groundwater extraction.
cases.management_lesson: Lake-surface monitoring should be paired with upstream dam inventory, groundwater pressure and agricultural demand.

cases.name: Poyang Lake
cases.observed_pattern: Changes in downstream river level and reservoir regulation increased the lake-river gradient and promoted faster outflow during key periods.
cases.management_lesson: A lake can lose water because its receiving river is hydraulically lower; inspect downstream controls and lake-river gradients, not only upstream supply.

cases.name: Chilika Lagoon
cases.observed_pattern: Reduced tidal exchange and ecological degradation were linked to channel shoaling and a shifting lagoon mouth.
cases.management_lesson: Test whether narrow connections, culverts, channels or outlets have lost hydraulic capacity before blaming only climate.

cases.name: Great Salt Lake
cases.observed_pattern: Declining levels are addressed through an integrated basin plan covering supply, demand, diversions, groundwater and water delivery to the lake.
cases.management_lesson: Build the management model at watershed scale; the lake alone is not the system.

cases.name: Salton Sea
cases.observed_pattern: Reduced inflow caused recession while salinity and nutrient concentrations increased, degrading habitat and water quality.
cases.management_lesson: Water quantity and quality must be monitored together; falling volume can concentrate pollutants and amplify ecological damage.

cases.name: Owens Lake
cases.observed_pattern: Diversions changed the basin water budget and the lake became predominantly dry except during unusually wet periods.
cases.management_lesson: Map every artificial diversion and export path when a terminal basin or wetland is losing water.

cases.name: Sahara — African Humid Period context
cases.observed_pattern: During the African Humid Period, large areas of today's Sahara supported more vegetation, wetlands and lakes; later hydroclimate shifted toward much drier conditions.
cases.management_lesson: Topography and basin geometry determine where water persists when climate shifts. Groundwater-fed desert depressions show why groundwater connectivity must be treated separately from surface rainfall.
cases.comparison_notice: Long-term paleoclimate benchmark, not a direct modern engineering analogue for Olszówka.

cases.name: Mono Lake
cases.observed_pattern: Water diversions beginning in 1941 lowered the lake level and exposed former submerged shoreline features.
cases.management_lesson: In an endorheic basin, small sustained reductions in inflow accumulate because evaporation is the only natural outlet.

cases.name: Lake Faguibine system
cases.observed_pattern: After drought dried the lakes, sand filled channels connecting them to the Niger; later rainfall could not fully restore inflow.
cases.management_lesson: A return of rainfall does not guarantee recovery if connecting channels have lost conveyance capacity. This is a strong analogue for testing local bottlenecks near Olszówka.

cases.name: Goose Lake
cases.observed_pattern: The lake repeatedly fills and dries; 2015 drying followed drought, while inflow also depends on irrigation diversions from feeder streams.
cases.management_lesson: Distinguish normal ephemeral behavior from structural decline by comparing multiple wet-dry cycles and upstream use.

cases.name: Lake Aibi
cases.observed_pattern: Three of five feeder rivers dried after upstream diversion; lake area fell sharply and exposed saline surfaces became dust sources.
cases.management_lesson: Remote sensing plus basin water allocation can identify whether upstream consumption is preventing ecological inflow; restoration must protect an explicit environmental water share.

cases.name: Puzhal Lake / Chennai reservoir system
cases.observed_pattern: In 2019, Chennai's rain-fed reservoirs approached empty conditions after a very weak monsoon and nearly 200 rainless days.
cases.management_lesson: For rainfall-dependent reservoirs, compare storage against seasonal precipitation and demand before inferring a local channel blockage.

cases.name: Mesopotamian / Iraqi Marshlands
cases.observed_pattern: The marshlands were almost entirely destroyed after drainage and upstream damming, followed by monitoring, reflooding and rehabilitation efforts.
cases.management_lesson: Hydraulic reconnection can restore wetland area in some systems, but restoration must be monitored and managed at basin scale rather than performed as an isolated excavation.

cases.name: Walker Lake
cases.observed_pattern: Much of the Walker River is diverted for agriculture before reaching the lake; reduced inflow accompanied major volume loss and rising salinity.
cases.management_lesson: A shrinking terminal lake can reveal both quantity and quality stress; quantify freshwater inflow needed to keep salinity within ecological thresholds.

cases.name: Lake Mead
cases.observed_pattern: During prolonged drought, inflow fell while water use and regulated outflow continued, producing sustained reservoir decline.
cases.management_lesson: For managed reservoirs, compare inflow, mandated releases, evaporation and demand; shoreline change alone cannot identify the cause.

cases.name: Lake Casitas
cases.observed_pattern: Storage fell below 30 percent after repeated droughts, then rebounded to full capacity after two wetter-than-normal winters.
cases.management_lesson: Use recovery after wet periods as a diagnostic: if a basin does not rebound when precipitation returns, search for structural loss of inflow, drainage or groundwater connectivity.

cases.name: Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre
cases.observed_pattern: Exceptional upstream rains can fill the normally dry basin; when tributaries weaken, evaporation rapidly exceeds inflow and levels fall.
cases.management_lesson: Terrain and episodic upstream runoff can dominate lake behavior. A naturally ephemeral basin is a control case against falsely diagnosing every drying event as infrastructure failure.
